title: India vs US Consumer
summary: A side-by-side of the Indian and US consumer for someone whose instincts were built in India: payments, delivery economics, retail formats, price sensitivity, households and digital habits. Shows how to turn India experience into an interview edge without assuming the US works the same way.

Credit and debit cards; ~82% of adults hold a credit card (2025)
Ubiquitous; credit score shapes renting, loans, even jobs

Less common; cards often paid in full

10-20 min grocery is mainstream in metros
Same-day or 1-2 hour slots; 15-min mainly in dense cores
Larger, planned baskets; minimums and fees

blocks.title: Why 10-minute delivery is rarer in the US
blocks.body: Three things break the Indian unit economics. Labor per hour costs several times more, and many cities set minimum pay for app couriers. Low density means fewer orders per square km, so a dark store sees fewer orders and riders travel farther, often by car. And US shoppers already stock up weekly with a car and a big pantry, so the 'forgot milk' occasion is smaller. Several US 15-minute grocery startups shrank or exited after 2022.

blocks.title: How to use India experience as an advantage
items: Lead with the mechanism, not the country: 'order density drives delivery cost per drop' travels; 'India does 10-minute delivery' does not.
Translate units: rupees to dollars, two-wheelers to cars, kirana to convenience store, before drawing a conclusion.
Flag the difference explicitly: labor cost, density and basket size, then say what would need to be true in the US.
Use India as a leading indicator for mobile-first payments, super-apps and low-price-point innovation.
Keep to one India example per answer; the interviewer wants your US judgment.

blocks.title: Example phrasings
items: "At a quick-commerce company in India, dark-store profitability hinged on orders per store per hour. In the US I'd first check whether this zip code has enough density to reach a similar number."
"In India UPI made payments nearly free for merchants; in the US interchange funds rewards, so a payments product needs a different value proposition."
"I've seen small packs widen reach in price-sensitive markets; for this US dollar-store case, I'd test smaller pack sizes for lower-income shoppers."
"I'd be careful generalizing from India here: US labor costs and car-based shopping change the math, so let me size it bottom-up."

blocks.title: Don't over-generalize either market
blocks.body: India is not one market (metro vs tier-2 vs rural differ hugely), and neither is the US (Manhattan vs suburban Texas). Avoid 'Americans always…' or 'Indians always…'. Compare specific segments, and be clear about which differences are structural (density, labor cost) vs cultural or temporary.

blocks.title: Turn it into a fit story
blocks.body: In fit interviews, frame India experience as range: you've built for consumers who are extremely price-sensitive and mobile-first, and you know how to question whether a model transfers. That signals adaptability and humility, which US consulting and tech interviewers value.

in_a_case: US quick-commerce entry: walk through density, labor cost and basket size as the three gates; conclude it works only in select urban cores.
Payments or fintech case: contrast near-zero merchant cost UPI with US interchange-funded rewards to explain why consumers are attached to cards.
CPG pricing for lower-income US shoppers: borrow the small-pack/price-point idea from India, but test against US retailer shelf economics.
Fit question 'Why does your experience matter here?': give one mechanism you learned in India and how you'd adapt it, not a list of India facts.
Delivery app profitability: in the US, fees, subscriptions, tips and ads carry the economics that density alone carries in Indian metros.
